Figure 1:Do capable models specify their own self-improvement?We give a frozen LLM (here,Claude Opus-5) the general goal of improving itself at gameplay, and place it in a constrained workspace. We do not provide real games to practice on, or prescribe a particular self-improvement loop. We instead provide a toolset{Read, Write, Bash, Gameplay}, and allow the teacher to generate its own games and organize its own learning procedure.
At the start (t=0t=0) the teacher uses its tools to build a test game, spawn a player session to play that game, analyze the result, and then update the player context (e.g., skill files). Later (t=60t=60), the teacher decides to write an adversarial game and observe the player attempt it with and without the optimized context. The teacher then uses the observed failure mode to make another context update.

Figure 2:Examples of evaluation benchmarks.Sample games from our transfer benchmark, ordered in increasing distance from our canonical self-optimization setting: (1)PuzzleScript(same game engine, different horizon splits), (2)ARC-AGI-3(different engine and representation), (3)MazeBench(3D navigation and mechanics in isometric ASCII projections).

header: 4What are the strategies of successful self-improvers?

images.caption: Figure 8:Excerpts from aClaude Opus-5teacher session with high alignment to self-regulated learning subprocesses.In the first example (task-strategies) the teacher writes a random level generator and BFS solver to filter generated games for difficulty and employs A/B testing to identify where its optimized text artifacts are useful. In the second (learning goal orientation) the teacher designs an adversarial game to test its advice and runs validation tests across earlier games to identify regressions.
